claims.text: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment can generate a coherent oxide layer on Q235 steel.
The induced oxide film is continuous and adherent.
The induced film is composed mainly of iron oxides such as Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
A continuous and adherent oxide film acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
At room temperature, the induced oxide layer remains stable.
At room temperature, the oxide layer slows the ingress of corrosive agents.
At elevated temperatures, thermal stresses can induce microcracking in the oxide layer.
Elevated temperatures can alter the oxide layer's phase composition.
Microcracking or phase-composition changes reduce the protective ability of the oxide layer.
Loss of oxide-film integrity accelerates corrosion.
At room temperature, pre-oxidized Q235 steel will exhibit a delayed onset of corrosion relative to untreated Q235 steel.
At room temperature, pre-oxidized Q235 steel will have a lower corrosion rate than the untreated reference.
At approximately 80°C, the protective effect of the pre-induced oxide film will diminish.
At elevated temperature, increased corrosion rates will coincide with observable oxide-film degradation such as microcracking or phase changes.
The proposed mechanism is applicable when oxygen, humidity, corrosive-agent exposure, and temperature are controlled in the laboratory.
The protective effect may not extrapolate to field conditions involving temperature extremes or strongly fluctuating atmospheric conditions.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis refers to 'pre-exposed Q235 steel,' whereas the specified initial state is clean, untreated steel before exposure. This creates ambiguity about whether the steel has already experienced environmental exposure or is merely pre-oxidized as part of the intervention.
